utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. The next witness is Dr. Antonio Alonso. His evidence is relevant to paragraph 75(D) Schedule (D), and 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. Now, you're receiving an interpretation in Spanish of what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Antonio Alonso Alonso.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, what are you by profession?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I am -- I work at the National Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Sciences at the Institute of Biology, and I am specialised in forensic biogenetics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And since when have you been working at the national Institute of Toxicology and Forensic Science?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Since 1984. So therefore it's approximately 25 years that I've been working at the biology service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And very briefly could you explain what are your duties and responsibilities at the institute where you're employed?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. Basically I work as an expert with the -- at the court, at the legal courts in the fields of genetics and forensic science with three specialisations, the identification of remains, and in criminal investigations through the study of the study of biological remains, and also in paternity analysis, the biological investigation of paternity. This is three main fields in the field of forensic genetics that I work at at the institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Exhibit 65 ter 02501 is your curriculum vitae, and I will not be going into detail since the document speaks for itself. It is a document that you provided to our Office of the Prosecution in 2003. I would like to know if there are any updates that you would like to make to your curriculum vitae, any recent changes to your professional occupation.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, apart from some other scientific studies which of course aren't listed from 2003 to now. I should point out that in Spain there is a new commission of recent creation for the forensic use of DNA. This is an organism that regulates quality issues, bioethical issues, legal issues, and scientific issues of the application of DNA in forensic sciences, and I have been appointed secretary of this commission. Also, in the last two years, I have taken part as an expert in another commission or committee that was set up to develop a national protocol for genetic identification for cases where there are major disasters. So these are the two most recent facts which are not in the CV you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the curriculum vitae, this is 02501, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned P00798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir you spoke about your duties at the Spanish forensic institute and you said that you worked in the field of genetic and forensic science. Is DNA testing done at the institute where you're employed, and if yes, what type of DNA testing is done there?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Basically, as I said before, the DNA tests are carried out for the purpose of identifying individuals, individuals who have disappeared, or persons who were victims of major disasters; and we also have vast experience in the identification of individuals through the identification of skeletal remains in mass graves. On other occasions we -- we have helped this court with -- in cases relating to the war in Bosnia, and we have also identified victims of the Spanish civil war which took place between 1936 and 1939. This, of course, is material which is far more difficult to work with than the material that we've been able to work for this court. In that case it's because the remains are very, very old. And we also work with another field in forensic genetics is the analysis of very old DNA, ancient DNA that may have even archaeological value. So our centre has a lot of experience, and we have really specialised in the genetic identification of skeletal remains of bones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And is the manner of DNA testing carried out by your institute consistent with industry standards presently?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: In the field of forensic genetics, there is a very high degree of standardisation in terms of the techniques that we can use or in the kind of genetic markers that can be applied to the different kinship relations, genetic kinship relations that we use. We also use systems that have been validated, and these are systems that are used by most of laboratories worldwide. So in brief, the reply is, yes, we do use standardised techniques that have been assessed. And throughout the process we also use a number of controls, positive and negative controls, which indicate how reliable the results are. Also, our centre also engages in a number of exercises to prove its worth, as it were. For example, there are controls carried out by the Spanish and Portuguese group of the -- Spanish and Portuguese group of the National Institute of Forensic Sciences and controls that are carried out with the European network of forensic science institutes. This is the European network that brings together all these institutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, did you prepare four reports on genetic identification of human skeletal remains that were exhumed in 2001 at a location called Batajnica in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand -- I'm sorry, I just got the interpretation. I understand that the last of these reports which is dated 17th November, 2004, contains a summary of the findings of the previous three reports and also some additional information regarding further testings that your institute was involved in with respect to these remains; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that is correct. The first three reports are partial reports in the sense that we received different reference samples, and in each of the reports we assessed the samples with samples from relatives that we had received; and the last report is a final report where we have all the results, but we also increase the number of genetic markers, which means that the identification is more reliable, because then the systems -- at the time we had then new systems with far more markers which are -- which make them more reliable. So this is the final report. It is complete as far as all the information that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- this report is 65 ter 02486. It is the report dated 17th November, 2004, and I seek to tender that into evidence. I will not be seeking to tender the first three reports for the reasons that have just been explained by the witness as these are contained within the final report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The report will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00799, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, in June of 2006, did you provide some responses to questions that were sent to you by the Office of the Prosecution in relation to the reports that you had prepared and also with -- were in relation to the methodology used by your institute in carrying out its DNA testing?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in these responses did you also explain various aspects of your reports?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. There are a number of aspects that have to do with the tasks and the functions of the institute. There's also explanations concerning the qualifications of the specialists that signed this report with the technical characteristics of the reports; also in terms of quality assurance measures; also with the systems and the standardised methods for the final statistical validation of the -- of the results obtained; also concerning the -- the custody of the samples, of the samples from the skeletal remains; and also the samples from the reference kinship samples. And this is -- these are all the replies that are presented in that later paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I seek to tender this exhibit into evidence. It is 65 ter 02487.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00800.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir did you also previously testify before this Tribunal in the case of Milutinovic et al.?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you recently had a chance to review the transcript of your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And having reviewed your testimony, would you provide the same answers to the questions that you were asked then if you were asked those questions today?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender the transcript of the Milutinovic case. This is 65 ter 05259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned P00801, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to now turn to your report, this is the fourth report from 2004, and ask you some questions about that. Could you -- could you first explain how it is that you became involved in the process of genetic identification of the remains that were exhumed from Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, Jose-Pablo Baraybar, an anthropologist, contacted the toxicology institute asking us if the institute might help with the genetic identification of different remains, including the remains from Batajnica, and I think that this was the first contact that we had. Afterwards, we received the samples from Batajnica. They were sent directly by the director of the Institute of Legal Medicine of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of the director of the Institute of Legal Medicine of Belgrade who sent these samples to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. It's Dr. Dusan Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your report you indicate that you received 56 samples from the Belgrade institute, and on page 1 of the report these samples have been identified with a code, a BA code and then a number. Was this number that was assigned to each one of the samples, this reference code, was this assigned by your institute or did the samples come pre-numbered with these -- this reference code from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: The samples had already been assigned these codes from Belgrade. You can see that in fact in the photograph of each of the containers that included -- containing the samples. There was this identification given to each -- to each of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were these samples sent to you? Did Professor Dunjic personally travel to Spain to deliver the samples or how were they sent to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Professor Dusan Dunjic personally took them to the National Institute of Toxicology.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in your report you also refer to receiving 13 blood samples of reference kin and 11 of which were received from the International Commission of Missing Persons and two from this Tribunal. Based on the material that you received from these different institutions, how many positive identifications were you able to make after you conducted your testing at the institute?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Now, there's a total of 21 identifications that were carried out on the basis of three kinds of DNA markers: autosomic inheritance markers, which are inherited at 50 per cent from the parents, the father and the mother. This also through mitochondrial DNA which is inherited only through matrilineal descent; and also there's the analysis of markers in the Y chromosome, which is inherited only patrilineally from fathers to sons. Now, we had analysed different kinship ties. Firstly, relating the samples to the remains to the reference samples. Some of the remains identified were also related to other remains to identify, as it were, chain reactions. It should be borne in mind that among these remains there are family groups, many of them with a considerable number of individuals within the same family group. And there are two cases where the analysis was done through mitochondrial DNA and Y chromosome testing, and in our previous report we had already said that since these kind of markers, mitochondrial DNA and Y chromosome, it was less discriminatory in nature that we -- that this should be considered as a preliminary identification, not as a proven or confirmed identification which would, however, be the case for the rest of the identifications indicated in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you referred to having been -- having made 21 identifications on the basis of three kind of DNA markers. What about the remainder of the 56 remains that you received? Why were you unable to identify the remainder of those human remains?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Firstly, I should say, that among the 56 remains we identified 41 different profiles. So it means that there are some individuals that are repeated among the samples. That's the first conclusion of this report that from the 56 samples of remains there are 41 individuals there. In fact, there are 10 individuals who are twice and 2 individuals who are there three times. That is, there are cases where there are three remains of the same individual and a number of cases where there are two remains, samples of remains of the same individuals. So the first thing is that from 56 presumed victims this figure would go down to 41, and that's in the report. We have only been able to compare these remains with 13 reference samples. It might well be that part -- that some of the non-identified individuals, they have not been identified because we did not have an appropriate reference sample. There might be other explanations. As, for example, that the 56 victims which the intention is to identify are not among these remains. We don't know what the whole previous work done on these samples was. The anthropological identification which allows a preliminary identification of these remains and thus we cannot know what the reasons are for the non-identification of the other remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In your report when you're speaking about these identifications, you refer to the expression "cannot rule out the possibility." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, yes. We say we cannot exclude the possibility of such and such an individual being the father or the son or the child of another sample. Having analysed 15 different regions of the DNA, in each of them we have identified the combat ability that might be expected from a father/son or parent/child relationship. Let us remember that this kind of DNA is inherited from parents to children, i.e., 50 per cent paternal genes and 50 per cent maternal genes. And for each of these regions, there's one variant that we receive from our fathers and -- and another variant we receive from our mothers. So what we're saying is that we cannot rule out this possibility because we see that there is compatibility for each and every one of these regions analysed. Once we have this compatibility for each of the regions, what we do is a statistical assessment of what the probability would be or what the degree of probability would be on the basis that these are indeed the presumed remains as compared to other remains. So this is what we call the likelihood ratio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And in your report you explained that in addition to receiving these remains and the blood reference samples of kin, you also received two documents, a family tree from the ICTY where the family ties between the reference samples and the Suva Reka massacre victims were found and also a table that you received from the International Commission of Missing Persons where again family ties between the difference samples and the victims of this massacre were shown. Can you explain how you used these two documents in the process of genetic identification of these remains?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. What we do, whether we do a comparative analysis once we have the genetic profiles of the reference samples and the samples of the skeletal remains, is to compare all of them, every single one, and we do this in -- using a blind system, as it were. And once we do that, we can have the genetic compatibility. Once we have the genetic compatibility, if we have one of the reference samples which is part of a family group, we evaluate whether this parent/child relationship identified corresponds to the theoretical information that we have from the family tree. So we try to see if the information that we obtain corresponds or matches the information that we have from the family tree and the information of that nature. So it's like a puzzle. We have different kinds of genetic compatibility, parent/child or siblings, for example. So we try to see them and try to check them and to match them with the family tree. And in all the cases, we have indeed established this genetic compatibility but also the relations, the kinship from the family tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you first examined the genetic compatibility and establish the family ties before relying on this, on the family tree and the document received from the commission of missing persons. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because this is done automatically. The databases using a software to carry out these comparisons which tell us between these remains and this reference sample a compatibility of 50 per cent is observed for each of these DNA regions. So this can well be a parent/child relationship. Once we have that, we go and check it in the family tree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the actual names of the victims that you were able to identify, those were obtained from the family tree. If I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. In most of the cases we obtained the names from the family trees, the different tables that we have. We have also received the names from the identification of the reference samples. There's one thing I wanted to say: The nomenclature used for the names is not always constant, not always constant, and we mentioned this briefly when we submitted the report, because sometimes or in most of the cases the nomenclature used is surname, then name of the father between brackets, and the given name at the end, but not always. There are some variations on this. Sometimes, for example, it's only the surname and the given name. So the nomenclature is not always wholly standardised. What we have done is to transcribe the information that we received in the family trees, basically, but also the reference samples are identified and it is these names that we have used for the identification of these samples.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the family tree and the document prepared by the International Commission of Missing Persons is 65 ter 02500. I'm not going to show it to the witness; he has already explained it. But I seek to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be assigned P00802.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Dr. Alonso, I would like to now move to the responses that you provided to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could have up on the screen page 8 of 65 ter 02487.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a table that is attached to the responses you prepared. In response to a question about the genetic profiles that were used in -- with regard to the populations that were used, you indicated that you had used European and Spanish population genetic profiles but that you had later recalculated these profiles based on a database of Kosovo Albanian individuals which had recently been published. If we have -- I would -- do you have the document up on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's right here before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like you to explain the last two columns which are marked LR1 and LR2. If you can explain what the values are contained in those columns represent?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Once we have determined the genetic compatibility between the two samples, what we do is we assess how many times more probable this is vis-a-vis the hypothesis that it is a relationship father/son, mother/daughter, and so on and so forth, vis-a-vis the hypothesis, that there is not that relationship and that it is two people who are not related genetically. Very well, in all the cases we see that that value - and I think in most of the cases it is above and beyond 10.000. What does this mean now? That it is 10.000 more probable that there is that compatibility than the hypothesis that there is -- in the hypothesis that there are two people related vis-a-vis the hypothesis that they aren't. When we say they are not related, what we do is we assess the general population and we see what the probability is that there's an individual who's compatible with this type of compatibility even if he's not genetically related. And, therefore, we need the genetic frequencies of the population. We've done two calculations. Number one with European frequencies, Caucasians from our own institute. And in 2004 we published a database with an Albanian -- Kosovo Albanian populations and we've recalculated indices. In every case there are variations, but from the point of view of final significance, it's not really important in all the cases. We are confirming here that there -- we're at or above an LR of 10.000. Now if we change, if we transform this data this information in terms of probability, of paternity, of maternity, one date of ORLR of 10.000 is equivalent to a possibility of paternity, of maternity of 99.99 per cent. An LR of a hundred thousand is equivalent to 99.999 per cent and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any changes in the identifications, or did this new -- use of the new database of the Kosovo Albanian population in your identification process, did that have any impact on your findings with relation to the identification? I'm sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I had realised the transcript had stopped, but I did not want to interrupt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you would wait before responding. I'll just repeat my question. The transcript was not working. Dr. Alonso, what I had asked was whether when you recalculated your results on the basis of this new database of the Kosovo Albanian population, if that had had any impacts on the genetic identification that you had carried out when examining these remains.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. In other words, the values are pretty much the same in terms of LR. The calculation has no significance for what we obtained before. Here we only assess the significance, the importance of that compatibility. And in all the cases, we have values that are to be expected or that would be expected. If we consider the relations identified as certain. Therefore, the reply is no, there are no significant variations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And given your experience and expertise in the area of DNA testing, can you tell us in your opinion is the DNA identification carried out by the Spanish -- by your institute, the Spanish forensic institute reliable to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty? I'm talking about the DNA testing with respect to the remains received from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, it's the degree of reliability that today's genetic technologies that we apply in this area of genetics allow us to arrive at. If you take a look, they are number -- certain numbers here, millions, hundreds of millions in terms of the coefficients and ratios, and that is because we have a reference sample and we have two individuals that could be the mother and the father. In other words, when we have the two parents and a child, the value of those coefficients is much higher and much more reliable than if we only have a mother or a father then the coefficients go down. I repeat that that is what we would expect in relation -- a kinship relation. We understand that beyond -- above and beyond an LR or coefficient of a thousand or 10.000, well, we have high possibility of paternity, at least sufficiently so, so as to say that they're practically proven identifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Alonso. Those are my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no further questions for the witness at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have some questions for witness. Just to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Alonso. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I am the Defence counsel for the accused, Djordjevic. I will have a couple of questions for you, not many. I merely want to clarify certain matters in your expert report which is otherwise of a very high level. You answered my learned friend's question concerning the 56 samples sent to you by Mr. Dunjic from Belgrade. We don't know why the mortal remains have not been identified, and this can be interpreted in several ways. Were these -- were you referring to 56 bodies, or were these actually mortal remains to -- referring to a larger number of bodies that originated from Batajnica? In other words, in addition to the 56 bodies, were there other samples as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: No. We refer to 56 pieces, units, individual units of skeletal remains. Each one in hermetically sealed container that we received and we know nothing more about them. We don't know to how many people they relate. From those 56 remains, these are 56 samples, after an initial analysis we see that there are 41 genetic profiles. Amongst the 56 remains there are 41 people represented there. That is the information we can give you as a consequence and as a result of our genetic testing. We do not know, we do not know how many victims are being looked for. We don't know whether as a result of the preliminary tests done, anthropological tests after the exhumation, there is an approximate idea of what the number of victims was or is. You must remember that we received a unit, a piece of large bone in most cases, so probably there's prior information from anthropological analyses that indicate, and perhaps not in a certain manner or a confirming manner, but that there's information regarding the number of victims to be expected. After the genetic tests of the 56 remains, we know that there are 41 individuals. I don't know whether I answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course. This is my follow-up question: Does this mean that the 56 remains you received, each and every one of the remains had been assigned a reference number and that had been assigned before the samples reached your hands, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Dr. Dunjic, the director of the forensic institute from Belgrade and Mr. Fulton from the ICTY were present -- or, rather, they were the ones who brought the samples over to you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did colleague Dunjic tell you at all or was it -- was it an assumption at the time that each and every one of these remains belonged to a different person?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I cannot exactly remember what he said, what Dr. Dunjic said at the time. The only thing they asked us to do was to analyse those remains. I don't know whether there was that idea that each one might come from a different individual, a different individual. Frankly, I cannot reply to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that among the 56 remains there were identical DNAs in respect on -- of some of the samples, or, rather, the DNA of a certain individual was found in several remains?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, there were 10 individuals of whom there were two samples or two remains, and two individuals I seem to remember of whom there were three, and the -- the rest, each matched a different individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There were 56 registered remains that were brought over to you, and you said that they were from long bones mostly. It can be assumed, and you'll agree with me, that Dr. Dunjic, in bringing over the different 56 samples bearing different reference numbers, presumed that each and every one of the remains belonged to a different person. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: It could be that way, but it could also be that, depending on the circumstances in which the remains are recovered, and depending on whether these are complete skeletons or not, it is very usual that there are doubts and that samples are taken from different parts so that through a technology that allows us to differentiate we differentiate. Oftentimes we receive samples without there being security or knowledge whether it is from different individuals or not, so there can be doubts. This all depends. It depends on the circumstances of the common grave, of the type of remains that are found, whether partial remains or they're complete skeletons, like I said. And therefore this is a difficulty, a primary difficulty in the area of analysis. So there are two reasons based on the supposition that there are 56 individuals or whether there are doubts as regards that they are or not 56 individuals. Like I said, that all depends on the difficulty surrounding the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my next question for you: Having received the evidence, the samples, did you also receive records which would show you from which location and in what way were the remains exhumed to which these reference samples belonged? Did you have any knowledge of these matters when conducting your analyses?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: We did not have any information of the details. We only knew the place, the remains from Batajnica, in other words, and we had an analysis -- or, rather, a chart with possible results, anthropological results, very general. They only identified who might be a man, who might be a woman. And in some cases, because amongst the victims there were children, there were infants, there was also the age, the possible age. Remember that these types of anthropological analyses are approximate analyses, they're not as reliable as the ones we're determining here today of genetic origin. They are only general. They give approximate ages. They point to the possibility of it being a woman or a man. This also depends on the number of remains found. This is the only information we had at the time. We knew the remains were coming from Batajnica, and we had a small chart pointing to the possibility of somebody being a woman or a man and the approximate age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm sorry. As indicated yesterday, we have to adjourn now. I'm afraid, Dr. Alonso, we must interrupt the proceedings for a time. There is a -- a special ceremony that the Judges must attend now. We hope to be able to resume sitting at 10.30, but that will depend precisely on the length of the ceremony. So we apologise for this interruption, but we will adjourn now and resume at 10.30 or as near after that as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alonso, further to what we discussed, I would like to know the following: Would it have helped you had you had complete reports of forensic anthropologists and forensic medicine specialists concerning the remains you received? That's to say, the remains of the individuals who were supposed to be identified.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, the job we did is blind, and that way that's why it gives warranties. We don't need to have that previous information. We obtain the genetic profiles and compare them. What could have been interesting in order to get a better degree of discrimination would have been if we had gotten more reference samples from family. That would have been helpful. But really, in these kind of cases, what we do is we -- we work blind. We access compatibilities, obtain the profiles, and then we compare it with the reference. We go to the trees, and there we can find the kinship relationship that we have identified between a remain and a reference sample and see how it fits within a genealogical tree. So what we do normally with genetic analysis is a comparative analysis that we do blind. For the combined assessment, and this doesn't apply only to this field, but for example for the identification of missing people in great catastrophes. In the end, it's good to actually integrate all the data that we can maybe obtain from radiological analyses, odontological, or genetical, or of prints. But here we have bone remains, and it wouldn't have really helped us since we actually this these -- they were bone remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the first contacts made with you for the work you did for the ICTY were made, in fact, by the forensic anthropologist, Mr. Baraybar. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. He was the one who got in touch with the National Institute of Toxicology, and he asked us whether we could actually carry out this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who was it who subsequently agreed with you that the first samples should be taken to Madrid? You said that it was Mr. Dusan Dunjic who came, the director of the Forensic Medicine Institute from Belgrade and Mr. Fulton, a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor at the time. But who was it who arranged for their arrival and their visit to your institute?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I do not know this information. It was both Professor Dunjic and Mr. William Fulton. Both of them actually arrived at the institute with the samples once the anthropologist told us that they were actually looking for a reputed lab in order to carry out these identifications and that they needed a given specialisation. This happened in 2002. And at that date, not too many labs had the experience we had actually with the analysis of bone remains. So it was actually both of them who established contact with Professor Baraybar, and they went to the institute. We agreed the date for the visit, and they came with the samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since at the time there still did not exist a laboratory in Serbia that would conduct the type of analysis you engaged in, did you engage in any preliminary arrangements with Professor Dunjic as to the type of samples that had to be brought along and the manner in which they were to be transported? In addition, did you discuss the manner in which the samples had to be designated, or was it all the result of an ad hoc arrangement?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I don't remember whether before we actually received these samples we actually had a contact with Dr. Dunjic. However, the samples we got from the way they were wrapped and the way they were presented, they were -- this was done in the right way in order to use them as evidence. It didn't look like anything was ad hoc, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On -- at several places in your report you mention the term "contamination." What does it exactly mean, the contamination of a sample?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Most of the samples with these many years usually allow for destruction of very small amounts of DNA. These amounts so -- are so small that they can actually be even smaller the amount that we can be in a droplet of a saliva when we speak. That's why we have to develop measures in order to avoid contamination and in order to monitor the possibility of detecting contamination. That's why before extracting DNA the remains are cleaned in the outside surface, in the marrow; as well, they're treated with UV light in order to destroy all possible contamination on the surface. We work under biological security bells in order to avoid contamination from the operator. We also wear special clothes and in a special area to carry out the analysis, which is actually independent, apart from the place where the DNA's extracted. In order -- in destructions of DNA, we actually carry out negative checks. And we do all this because we work with a very small amount of DNA. The technique we use in order to get the profiles, we use the polymerase chain reaction, that technique. That technique allows us to amplify quite an important amount of DNA from a very small. And in this process, if we have any contamination, this contamination will be amplified as well. That's why all this work is done this way in order to avoid contamination and also to monitor whether there has been or not some contamination. The DNA was quantified. All the negative checks were negative. All the samples gave us amounts of DNA that were actually above the amount needed with today's techniques.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you extract the DNA from the compact tissue of the bone or from the dental material contain in the samples that were brought over to you? Secondly, the samples that were delivered to you, did they exhibit any signs of contamination that may have originated from the time before they came into your hands? And did they exhibit any signs of external -- externally inflicted defects, destruction, or anything of the sort which may have had a bearing on the identification process you embarked on to establish who the samples belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: As regards the first question, we extracted DNA through -- from the compact tissue. We did not actually have any dental tissue. Dental samples are actually the best DNA, but so is the compact tissue. The samples we received showed the contamination normal for these kind of samples. These are bone remains that actually have gone through a rotting process that had destroyed the soft tissue. So there is actually bacterial contamination. However, this doesn't affect our analysis, because we only analyse the human DNA. We didn't see any external sign of tampering or destruction of any handling of the samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The autopsy reports which those of us involved in the case had access to, I'm not sure if you had them at your disposal, but, for example, in the Sterenberg Jon report, there is reference to the corpses exhumed from Batajnica, and since I learned from my colleagues who are also experts in this field, I understood that any sort of burning to which remains may have been exposed to could make DNA identification impossible, I would like to know whether any of your samples exhibited any marks of burning or anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: No. At least in the samples we got, in the bone remains we got, we could not see signs of burning. I don't have any knowledge of the autopsy reports. However, when a bone is burned, and it depends on the degree of this burn, sometimes it can be impossible to actually be able to extract any DNA from such remains. What we had was a compact tissue, the normal bone colour, and we didn't see any signs of burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to call up Exhibit D003-0379.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the statement you gave on the 15th of November, 2008.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, is this the statement you gave, and do you recall giving the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show page 1 to the witness, please? This is all in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me assist you, Doctor. This is your statement where you spoke of Batajnica, as well as of the Glodjane location. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I do remember. This is my signature. I remember the questions from this interview are not related to the samples from Batajnica that were also taken by Professor Dunjic to Madrid and that they were -- they had different features regarding identification and regarding the state of the remains, so we couldn't proceed with a DNA test. They were left in custody. I think this is related to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is related to this case in terms of the way the investigations into the Kosovo crimes were conducted. What I'd like to know is, At the time when Dr. Dunjic delivered the mortal remains received in Glodjane in Kosovo, whether he was also accompanied by Mr. Fulton, Mr. William Fulton.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at which point did you establish that the Glodjane remains were contaminated to such an extent that they would not allow for any sort of DNA analysis to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: At -- we did not establish that they were so contaminated that they couldn't actually -- contaminated that they couldn't be -- go through a DNA test. What we said is that these samples were not the most appropriate samples since it was not compact tissue. It wasn't bone, but it was soft tissue that in cases was completely rotten. And also, some of the containers had somehow not too reliable identification. There were some codes that were crossed over with -- and then they had another code that didn't correspond to the first one. So what we did, we just kept these samples in custody, and we put them -- we made them available to the Tribunal. But it doesn't mean that we cannot actually get results from these samples. What I'm saying is that the DNA is going to be deteriorated, and it will be harder to carry out the tests. And in some cases, for example when it was only soft tissue, due to the high degree of the decomposition, we might not be able to get any information out of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I misunderstood this part, but quite understandably so. I am a layperson. Thank you for your explanation. At point 6 of your statement you say that you received the remains from Batajnica with a view to identifying the kinship relationships of the individuals whose mortal remains were given to you. You state there that you weren't given or provided any details. What did you refer to precisely there, that you did not receive any possible indication of the identities, of the identities of their family members, or something quite different? Can you explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: When we received the remains, all we knew was that they were remains from a common grave, that genetic analysis was to be done, and that we had some idea as to who could be the victims. And we also got reference samples in order to establish identity. That was all the information we had at the moment, the number of samples that we registered at the centre and the need to carry out a genetic analysis in order to do comparison with reference samples that we would be getting later as we got these samples over time. That's all the information we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clearer now. At page 10 of your statement, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at paragraph 10 of your statement at page 3, you say that you had expected to receive only the samples from Batajnica, and you were surprised to find that you had been furnished with the Glodjane samples as well. Can you tell us why were you surprised to receive both the Batajnica samples and the Glodjane samples, and how did it come about that you in fact received samples from Glodjane? Did you ask any additional explanation as to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, I was surprised in the way that the institute was expecting concrete, specific samples, and then on top of these samples we got another set of samples. That, as I said, the institute took pictures of them and kept them frozen in custody, and they are available for the use of the Tribunal. And we didn't analyse them because it was stated in this report and for other aspects that I -- actually we have communicated to the Tribunal. So our centre was expecting some samples, then another set of samples arrived. That's why we were surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to clarify. When your services were hired, I suppose that the discussions taking place between your institute and the ICTY went along the lines of the fact that you would be provided with some samples. Can you tell us something about these discussions that took place and how come -- were you given any sort of explanation as to why you received the Glodjane samples since Mr. William Fulton, a representative of the ICTY, was present at the hand-over?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly what the conversation was at that point. What we did make clear both to Professor Dunjic as to Mr. Fulton was that we were waiting for or expecting the Batajnica samples and that the other samples, of which we had had no knowledge before receiving them, that we would keep them in custody; but I said there were samples, there was a lot of decomposition, putrefaction, that we would keep them frozen. Years afterwards we were asked by the Tribunal about those samples. We gave the relevant explanations, and I think that these samples were then analysed by the International Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to know in relation to the material received is as follows: For the purpose of your analyses, were you given any sort of a court order, an ICTY order when it came to the Batajnica samples or not? In other words, is there a court order to the effect that you should analyse these remains?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you received an interpretation of the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, I didn't hear the interpretation into Spanish of the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the interpreters to tell me if I should repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer is yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: For the reference bone samples from the Batajnica location, did you receive a court order to conduct your analyses of those samples in line with the highest quality standards employed by your institute?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you could call it a court order, but certainly there was interest from the Tribunal and from -- this had been expressed in our correspondence that this analysis should be carried out. This concerning, for example, with the reference samples that they sent us or with the family trees that they had also sent us. There was interest from the Tribunal that we should carry out these analyses, but there was also Professor Dunjic. So there was, on the one hand, this question from the institute in Belgrade, but there was also clear interest from the Tribunal. So there was a request. There was a request that was made, and the fact that ICTY sent us the reference samples, the additional information, the family trees so that we could carry out the investigations will show clearly that there was an interest there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Dunjic ever send you reference samples of the Glodjane remains, the genealogical trees, and samples of the closest relatives of those whose remains were found in Glodjane and the samples of which remains you had in your possession at the institute?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: At no -- at no time. Neither information or family trees nor reference samples from possible relatives of the victims, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did this Tribunal ever show any interest for the Glodjane remains that were sent to you by Dr. Dunjic and Mr. Fulton?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes. A Prosecutor from the Office of the Prosecutor at some point requested information, had asked us for information on those samples and whether analysis could be carried out. We provided them with the information and documentary information of the samples and the state they were in, and we recommended that it should be -- that analysis should be carried out by a laboratory with a high -- with a lot of experience in performing analysis on this kind of sample, on these very difficult samples. And we even suggested that it should be the international commission that should carry out these samples because of the high degree of difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was the name of the Tribunal employee, Mr. Fernando Triana?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I think that this was the Prosecutor, the Spanish Prosecutor, who told us on the phone that there might be an interest in these samples. I can't remember exactly, but I think that was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My next question concerning the Glodjane remains is as follows: In item 22 of your statement, you say that the same year that you were contacted by Mr. Triana, that is to say 2006 in March, there was also an investigator of this Tribunal who came, Mr. Harjit Sandhu, who came to Madrid personally. You also state that you handed over to him the reference samples from Glodjane which he took away. Did I understand that correctly? Could you please clarify that? That is item 22 and 23 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: It wasn't the reference samples, it was the samples of the bone remains. These were the own samples that the institute had, and these were given with the relevant custody document to Harjit Sandhu from the Tribunal, investigator from the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After that you were contacted by Mr. Patrick Lopez-Terres inquiring about the samples once they had already left the institute. What was it all about, and who did Mr. Terres work for? This is in item 23 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Now, I don't remember exactly who Mr. Lopez-Terres worked for. I imagine that he worked for the Tribunal. Now, normally when we explain technical issues to people who have -- well, who have no specialised knowledge of the matter, sometimes there are difficulties in terms of understanding. If you see that there's contamination, bacterial contamination or through fungi, people understand that no, it will not be possible at all to obtain DNA. This is not always the case. When we tried to explain at the time that these were samples which -- for which we couldn't ensure that there would -- the guarantee that there would be success in obtaining DNA, that it might be very difficult to obtain nuclear DNA, which is the kind of DNA which is mostly used for this kind of identification. But it might be possible to obtain, let's say, mitochondrial DNA, which is less affected by this kind of contamination by microorganisms. It was this kind of technical explanation that we provided, and this was given together with documentation concerning these samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Answering my questions today, some ten minutes ago you said that once you handed over the mortal remains from Glodjane to the investigator of the Tribunal, that you advised them that the remains could better be analysed given the type of evidence, i.e., that these were not bones but, rather, soft tissue, that a different location would be better suited to analyse them. Which particular scientific institution did you have in mind when you offered that advice?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, I had said this before. We meant basically the laboratories of the International Commission for Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably so. I may have omitted that or failed to understand it. My next question is this: Do you know what the fate was of the remains? Do you know what became of them and what happened with them after you handed them over to the Tribunal representative?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: No, I have no official knowledge of what the ultimate fate of those remains was, but I am a scientific colleague of one of the people responsible for forensic analysis at the International Commission for Missing Persons, Dr. Thomas Parsons; and it is my understanding that these samples were, indeed, analysed at the labs of the International Commission for Missing Persons, but I have no official knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Alonso, considering the type, the reference samples were taken from family members, what is the actual importance of that procedure for the job you undertook?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The way the reference samples were taken from family members for whom it was presumed were next of kin to those who had been killed, be it in this instance or in some other cases of disasters, the way they are taken, how important is it? How important is the procedure itself for the overall task you aim to conduct?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Well, of course it is important, and there are two things that are basically important when taking a sample. On the one hand, that the biological sample is to be adequately preserved. Mostly, for example, it's blood samples which are placed on a filter paper and where there's a sufficient quantity to make it possible to obtain DNA reliably and to carry out two analyses, in fact. That's one thing. Secondly, the second thing is the identification of the individual from which the sample has been taken and the chain of custody. In all cases we received samples that had been taken adequately with the appropriate kits, that the containers had been sealed, which we then opened at the laboratory, having inspected the material, the documentation, and so forth. Now, of course the taking of the sample is a very important moment in terms of the identification of the person from whom it was obtained. It is this sample that will be used for the identification, and also again the state of preservation of the sample that is free from any contamination, et cetera, is of particular importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will go back to the analyses of mortal remains you undertook concerning the Batajnica remains. You said that you received those reference samples as well as family trees at a later point. As part of what procedure did you obtain those reference samples? Was that through direct contact with your lab, or did you simply get by those samples because they were sent on your request without any additional procedure?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: I seem to remember that in each of the reports that we submitted, and I think the first one was done using mitochondrial DNA with only one reference sample, we had said there once again that we needed more reference samples in order to be able to identify the other samples. All these samples were sent either by FedEx, by courier. They were FedExed or sent by DHL. And I have already said that they arrived in containers which were sealed and perfectly identified. And in our internal -- in our reports on the receipt of these samples there are no comments. There's nothing to point out concerning the state of these samples, the state in which they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who took those reference samples, and who was the person to send them to you? I suppose they came from the same institution.

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Of the 13 samples that we received, 11, they are -- there's a custody document with the whole -- with all these references. This is from the International Commission for Missing Persons. And two of the samples came directly from this Tribunal. The Tribunal has these documents, and there it is possible to see exactly who it was that took these samples, and the whole chain of custody until they arrived at the lab, and each of these samples, the documentation is signed as well by the person who took the sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question for you today has to do with the mortal remains from Glodjane. Once you handed them over to the Tribunal investigator Mr. Harjit Sandhu, did you hand them over according to prescribed procedure in order to spare them of possible contamination, putrefaction, or any other processes of that nature?

utterances.speaker: ANTONIO ALONSO
utterances.text: Yes indeed. These samples were quite contaminated already. This contamination from microorganisms is putrefaction, but in any case we prepared -- these samples were delivered in a fridge, in a refrigerator, ice box so as to avoid the -- as much as possible this contamination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I will not have any additional questions for you today. I thank you for the clarifications you provided for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that the witness statement of the 15th of November, 2006, be admitted into evidence. It is D003-0379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that will be assigned D00118, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. Kravetz, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have no re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, you'll be pleased to know that completes the questions of you today. The Chamber is grateful that you were able to come to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give and for the detailed reports that you have prepared and which we now have a greater understanding of. You may, of course, now return to your normal affairs, and we thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness is ready, Mr. Behar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next witness will be Tahir Kelmendi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We gather there may be some problem with reading in the case of the witness. Is this a matter of an eyesight difficulty or --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can indicate I'm not entirely sure. There does seem to be an eyesight difficulty. Mr. Kelmendi informed us that he does not have glasses either. So I think if -- if things could be read to him that would certainly be the most convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you sincerely and solemnly affirm that the evidence you will give will be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you, but first it may become very difficult for you to hold that earphone the whole time. If both are pulled in -- oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, sir. Thank you very much for coming here today. Can you please state your full name and your date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I am Tahir Kelmendi. I was born on the 21st of April, 1954, in Qyshk, Peja municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand that you're still living in Qyshk. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that on the 22nd of May, 2008, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you experienced in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to have that statement read to you before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: The -- the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor when we were in your proofing session, did you have a chance to go through that statement with an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I understand that there are a few things in that statement that you'd like to correct so that it accurately reflects your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can I have up on the screen 65 ter number 05135, please. And I'll be dealing first with paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 6 I understand that there may be an issue with the date. I'll just read the section to you. You state: "I remember that on the 25th of April ... the Serbian police came to our village asking to hand over weapons because nobody would ever harm us, and they received one legal held short gun and one hunting rifle, since we didn't have any other weapons in the village." Is that date mentioned there correct or does that require a correction?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: The date has to be corrected though. It was on the 17th and not on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you, sir, and I think that's clear. Let me take you to one more correction?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If we could have paragraph 75 up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: In this paragraph, and again I can read it to you, sir, you're describing the killing of Avdi Berisha that you observed. You described him being shot by what seemed to be a sniper. And this statement says: "This particular killing of Avdi Berisha I saw from a distance of not more than 30 metres. I was just on the other side of the stream where Avdi got killed." Is that distance correct or is there a correction or clarification that you'd like to make?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: The distance is 3 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So it's 3 metres and not 30 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, are you satisfied that the information that's contained in your statement is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00803.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can now provide a brief summary for the Court of Mr. Kelmendi's evidence. Mr. Kelmendi was born and raised in Cuska. He'll describe how in the early hours of the 14th of May, 1999, he observed Serbian police and VJ surrounding and then entering his village. He will explain that he recognised some of those police officers, including a Mr. Obrnovic, commander of the Klicina police station. He explains how he had seen and spoken with some of these police officers in the recent past. Mr. Kelmendi hid and observed an unfolding massacre and deportation. He watched as the Serb forces separated the men from the women and children. The women were sent to one house where they geared in the courtyard as the house itself was set on fire. He observed as the Serb forces divided the men and sent them in three groups to three different houses, 15 men to the house of Azem Rexha, 12 to the house of Sadik Gashi, and 10 to the house of Deme Gashi. He heard shootings in each of the houses. He then saw Serb forces set fire to those houses using flammable cartridges. He watched as the forces then took the women and children out of the courtyard and loaded them onto tractors, sending them out of the village to Peja. After the Serb forces left, Mr. Kelmendi was confronted with the bodies of his friends, neighbours, and relatives. He helped to hide those bodies, and then to bury them in a large grave. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I do have some questions for you. I'm going to have a number of questions about the 14th of May and the events on that date. I do first have a couple of questions for you about what happened before that day. At paragraph 36 of your statement, you explain that on the 13th of March -- actually, pardon me, the 13th of May, in the evening, about 80 refugees came to Cuska from the neighbouring village of Katundi i Ri, and you described that a man named Ranko Vlahovic had been in Katundi i Ri and had told these refugees to come to Cuska because Serbian please would be sending all of the Cuska villagers to Albania the next day. My question for you, sir, is can you tell us how it was that you learned that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: These things were told to me by someone who came there from the Katundi i Ri.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please ask the witness to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I'll just ask you if you can, we have microphones here, if it's possible if you can speak a little bit more closely to the microphone. And we did receive your answer for the last question so that's fine, but I will have some further questions for you. Could I ask you then, did you see these refugees yourself when they came to Katundi i Ri?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you mentioned that these things were told to you by someone who came from Katundi i Ri. Is this one of the refugees that you've described?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: This person is from Katundi i Ri. Suf Tafilaj is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You also -- you described this man Ranko Vlahovic. Can you tell us who was Ranko Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Ranko Vlahovic was the commander of the police station in Ozdrim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Even before what happened in this village, I used to know this person. I sat with him. I have talked with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I have some questions now for you about the events on the 14th of May itself. You described that at 6.00 a.m. on that morning you were out taking your cattle to the field. You described seeing police and VJ or army surrounding your village, and you described seeing Serb forces coming from the direction of Peja. Can you tell us how far Peja was from your village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Peja is about three kilometres away from Qyshk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you described the uniforms that you saw these forces wearing. You explained in your statement that the Serb forces were wearing camouflage, either with prevailing blue or with prevailing green colours, and you also described them wearing black bandannas and what sounded like face paint. I wonder, can you describe what you mean by that, what they had on their faces that you observed?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: The colour was black with green on the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You had described seeing Serbian police patrolling the Peja road in police cars, and you described recognising one of those officers as a man named Obrnovic. This is in paragraph 24. Can you explain to the Court who Mr. Obrnovic was and how you recognised him?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I used to know Obrnovic even before that case, because I had contacts with him. He was a very familiar face to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you tell us who he was, what his position was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Obrnovic was commander of the Klicina station, police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you say that you had contacts with him. Can you explain that for the Court a little bit? Had you spoken with him in the past?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Not that day, because it was impossible for anyone to approach him that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that, but how about in the past, in these --

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: In the past, yes. In the past, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you explain the contacts you had had, just briefly, the contacts you had with him in the past? Had you spoken to him before?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: In the past?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I was a farmer and always ran into him on my trips to and from Peja, so I knew him personally. I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in paragraph 27, you describe as well that the day before, that would be on May 13th, Mr. Obrnovic had sent another man named Mijo Brajovic to find out whether the villages in Cuska were armed and whether there was any police presence. Can you tell us how you know that -- how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I know this because at 2.00 in the afternoon of the 13th, with Mijo Brajovic I talked. He said to me, "Don't be afraid, because nothing will happen to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you explain what did you understand him to mean by that when he was telling you not to be afraid? What would you have been afraid of?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: As villagers that we were, we shouldn't be afraid of the forces when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brajovic tell you himself that Mr. Obrnovic had sent him?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did you know as well Mr. Brajovic from before? Was he someone that you had known before you spoke to him on this occasion that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And just before we move on, I know you mentioned the Klicina police station that Mr. Obrnovic was the commander of, can you tell us where the Klicina police station or where this town was in relation to Cuska, your village?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: It must be about 6 or 7 kilometres away from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. And how about Ozdrimi?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Ozdren is on the other side. It links Mitrovica with Peja. It's another -- this is another station that links Peja with Prishtina. This Klicina is on the road Prishtina-Peja. Ozdren is on the road that links Mitrovica with Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe in your statement that civilians in your town were gathered in the centre of the village, and you described in paragraph 41 that you didn't go there to the centre of the village, that you were watching from about 50 metres away. Can you explain to the Court where you were watching from?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I was 50 metres away from what was happening. After the house of Deme Gashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And when you say "after the house of Deme Gashi" - that's how it was interpreted to us - were you on the other side of the house, or can you explain more where you were?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: I was behind the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You described, as well, that the men were separated from the women. Can you explain how this was done, how they were separated?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: The police forces separated men from women when they came to the village. They asked them to hand over their identity cards, to throw on the ground their money, everything they had on them, the jewellery, everything. Then after that they separated them in three groups. The first group they sent to Azem's house, the second to Sadik Gashi's, and the third to Deme Gashi's where I was -- behind which I was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Now, I'll have some detailed questions for you about what happened next. Let's deal first with the group of women that you've mentioned. And first, can I ask where were the children? Were there children there as well?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And where were the children divided? Were they divided as part of that group as well?

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
utterances.text: Yes. The women and the children were sent to Sali Rexha Gashi's house. They were burnt. And then they put these people in Sali Rexha Gashi's house --

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TAHIR KELMENDI
